raw_text:
**Introduction and Clinical Rationale**
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of global cardiovascular mortality. While traditional transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (TV-ICDs) have successfully mitigated SCD risk, their reliance on intravascular leads presents significant long-term vulnerabilities, such as lead fracture, systemic bloodstream infections, venous occlusion, and pocket-related complications [1]. To address these structural pitfalls, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed, utilizing an entirely extrathoracic electrode and pulse generator [1]. The landmark, randomized PRAETORIAN trial established the long-term non-inferiority of S-ICD therapy compared to TV-ICDs in patients without pacing indications regarding the composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [2]. A subsequent secondary analysis of the PRAETORIAN trial further highlighted that lead-related complications and systemic infections are significantly less frequent and less severe with S-ICD compared to TV-ICD systems [3]. Additionally, the ATLAS trial demonstrated a major reduction in perioperative lead-related complications (such as hemothorax, pneumothorax, or cardiac perforation) with S-ICD compared to TV-ICD, emphasizing its acute safety advantages [4].

**Clinical Evidence and Safety Registries**
The real-world clinical performance of the S-ICD has been extensively documented in large safety registries. The international EFFORTLESS registry has tracked long-term clinical and patient-reported outcomes over a five-year follow-up period, confirming a sustained safety profile, with low complication rates and high shock conversion efficacy [5]. Midterm results from this registry documented the clinical learning curve and device performance during initial adoption [6]. Furthermore, pooled database analyses combining patients from the S-ICD investigational device exemption (IDE) study and the EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated that S-ICD therapy reliably detects and terminates spontaneous ventricular fibrillation events across a broad, heterogeneous patient population [7], confirming the initial safety and effectiveness established during the system's IDE evaluation [8].

**Managing Inappropriate Shocks**
Inappropriate shocks were historically a critical limitation of S-ICD therapy, occurring primarily due to cardiac oversensing (such as T-wave oversensing) or extracardiac noise [9]. To combat this, electrocardiographic (ECG) screening across different patient postures remains mandatory to evaluate repolarization and QRS/T-wave ratios before device selection [10]. Technical innovations have introduced advanced sensing algorithms, most notably the SMART Pass filter, which selectively filters low-frequency signals to prevent T-wave oversensing without compromising ventricular fibrillation detection [11,12]. Moreover, standardized programming, as evaluated in the UNTOUCHED trial, which implemented high-rate detection zones and dual-zone discrimination, has dramatically reduced inappropriate shock rates to levels matching or beating contemporary TV-ICDs [13]. To optimize device position post-implantation, clinicians employ the bidirectional chest radiograph-based PRAETORIAN score, which provides a non-invasive estimate of defibrillation success, serving as a reliable surrogate for intraoperative defibrillation threshold testing [14,15].

**Patient Selection and Guidelines**
International guidelines from the AHA/ACC/HRS [16] and the ESC [17] recommend the S-ICD as a Class I or IIa indication for patients with a standard ICD indication who do not have pacing, anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) needs [18]. S-ICD therapy is highly advantageous in young patients who face a high lifetime cumulative risk of transvenous lead failure and extraction complications [19]. Comparative propensity-matched cohorts have shown that S-ICD patients achieve comparable or superior long-term survival and lower complication-related morbidity compared to TV-ICD recipients [20], with similar clinical outcomes observed across both genders [21]. The S-ICD is also a superior choice in patients at high risk of systemic infection, such as those on chronic hemodialysis or with limited vascular access [22,23]. Additionally, in patients with non-functional transvenous systems, transitioning to an S-ICD following transvenous lead extraction is highly effective and safe, allowing continued defibrillation support while avoiding the risks of secondary transvenous leads [24,25].

**Surgical Techniques and Patient Comfort**
Implantation techniques have matured significantly to maximize both efficacy and patient comfort. Although the S-ICD can be safely implanted without fluoroscopy using anatomical landmarks [26], careful optimization of generator position is essential. Placing the device in an intermuscular pocket between the latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior, rather than a superficial subcutaneous pocket, improves cosmetic outcomes, reduces the risk of erosion, and yields more favorable PRAETORIAN scores [15]. To manage postoperative discomfort, regional anesthetic techniques, specifically the serratus anterior plane block, are increasingly employed [27].

**Emerging Frontiers: Modular Rhythm Management**
The historical limitation of the S-ICD has been its inability to deliver ATP or pacing. This gap is being systematically resolved through the integration of modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) systems [28]. In these systems, an S-ICD operates in tandem with a leadless pacemaker (LP) implanted in the right ventricle [29]. The two devices utilize wireless, intrabody communication to deliver synchronized pacing therapies. The landmark MODULAR ATP global trial successfully demonstrated that this dual-device system safely and effectively delivers pain-free ATP to terminate ventricular tachycardia and provides rate-responsive pacing, expanding S-ICD eligibility to a broader patient base [30].
